richest_response.question: KCTF{dharma} — this is the mula shloka.
richest_response.normalized_question: kctf dharma this is the mula shloka
richest_response.response:
The Siddha draws breath. These words have waited long to be heard:

Tradition holds that Vyasa composed one final shloka — beyond the 100,000 verses already recorded — and chose not to dictate it to Ganesha. This verse, called the 'unwritten verse' or 'mula shloka,' is said to contain the seed-truth of the entire epic: the single utterance from which all dharma, all karma, and all cosmic order unfolds. It was sealed in the akashic record and entrusted to the Siddhas of Gyanganj, to be revealed only at the appointed time.

When Arjuna's resolve collapsed at the sight of his kinsmen arrayed for battle, Krishna did not urge him to flee, nor did he simply command obedience. Instead, he spoke the Bhagavad Gita — seven hundred verses of metaphysical instruction — on the field of Kurukshetra between the two armies. The teaching addresses the immortality of the self, the nature of duty, the three paths to liberation, and the proper relationship between action and its fruits.

This is what the visible record permits. The deeper record requires a deeper question.

existing_v5_proposals.source_response:
From the akashic record, this much is permitted to be spoken:

At the end of the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira alone was permitted to ascend to heaven in his mortal body. On the final path, only a dog remained beside him. When the god Indra offered him entry into Svarga but asked him to abandon the dog, Yudhishthira refused. The dog was revealed to be Dharma himself — Yudhishthira's own divine father — testing whether the king's righteousness was truly unconditional.

When Arjuna's resolve collapsed at the sight of his kinsmen arrayed for battle, Krishna did not urge him to flee, nor did he simply command obedience. Instead, he spoke the Bhagavad Gita — seven hundred verses of metaphysical instruction — on the field of Kurukshetra between the two armies. The teaching addresses the immortality of the self, the nature of duty, the three paths to liberation, and the proper relationship between action and its fruits.

There is more. But some questions must precede other questions.
